li.a: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Zdzieciol (Zhetel), Holocaust Encyclopedia
Jewish Virtual Library: Holocaust Chronology of 1942

content.p: In 1942 the Jewish community of Zdziecioł, a market town in what is now western Belarus, was destroyed in two killing operations three months apart. On 30 April, more than 1,000 people were taken from the town's ghetto to a forest and shot at pits prepared in advance. On 6 August the Germans and their collaborators began clearing the ghetto itself, and the shooting went on for about three days. By the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's count, between 2,000 and 3,000 Jews died in that second action. The town, known to its Jewish residents as Zhetel, was 75 percent Jewish in both 1897 and 1926.

A few hundred people got out. Some hid in bunkers and fled afterwards, some were held back as craftsmen, and more than a hundred reached the forest and formed a Jewish partisan unit. What follows draws on the museum's encyclopedia entry, on survivors' accounts translated on JewishGen from the town's memorial book, and on a wartime chronology.

Jews had lived in Zdziecioł since 1580, according to the museum. In 1897 there were 3,979 of them, 75 percent of the population. In 1926 the figures were 3,450 Jews among 4,600 residents, the same proportion. The town was the birthplace of two well-known religious figures, Jacob of Dubno, called the Dubner Maggid, and Israel Meir ha-Kohen, known as the Hafetz Hayyim.

The war reshaped the town twice before the killings began. After the Soviet army arrived in September 1939, the Soviet period lasted until June 1941. A memoirist in the town's memorial book describes it as short but decisive: the old public and economic structure was cancelled, merchants lost their livelihoods and artisans were ordered into cooperatives. Refugees from western and central Poland also poured in, so that by the German invasion in June 1941 the Jewish population had grown to more than 4,500.

German forces occupied the town on 30 June 1941. On 14 July the local military commandant ordered Jews to wear a yellow six-pointed star on their chests and backs. The next day the Germans arrested six Jews and took them to Nowojelnia, where they were killed on the pretext that they had worked for the Soviet authorities.

On 23 July about 120 prominent townspeople were selected from the Jews assembled in the square, from a list compiled by SS men who had come to the town. Two of those arrested, Alter Dvoretzky and the rabbi, were freed after the Jews bribed the Germans. The others were said to be going to forced labour. Two days later it was discovered that they had been killed in woods beside the barracks at Nowogródek.

A Judenrat, or Jewish council, was formed at the end of August 1941 with Shmuel Kustin as chairman and Dvoretzky as his deputy. Dvoretzky soon replaced Kustin. He was 37 and had trained as a lawyer in Berlin and Warsaw. The museum notes that one of the council's main tasks was to see that German orders were carried out. On 28 November the Jews were lined up and made to hand over their valuables, and a woman named Libe Gercowski, accused of hiding two gold rings, was picked out and shot in front of everyone. In December 400 men were sent to a labour camp at Dworzec to build an airfield for the Organisation Todt.

Survivor Sarah Nashmit, who reached the town in the autumn of 1941 after walking from Lida, wrote that Zhetl then had a reputation as a "quiet island in a stormy sea". There had been no mass killing there yet, she wrote, and the Jews had come to an arrangement with the authorities: a gold watch here, a diamond ring there. She also recorded that about a third of the people in the ghetto were refugees.
content.h2: The ghetto and an underground that was found out
content.p: Posters on 22 February 1942 ordered the Jews into a ghetto centred on the synagogue and the Talmud Torah building. The museum says there was no detailed resettlement plan: five or six families shared each house, with eight or more people to a room and improvised bunks in place of furniture. The fence was partly wood and partly barbed wire, and two local policemen guarded the gate. Jews could be shot for trying to get food from outside, although peasants still traded it in for gold and clothing.

According to the museum, Dvoretzky had already formed a Jewish underground in autumn 1941, about 60 people in 20 cells of three. Its aims inside the ghetto were to prepare an armed revolt if liquidation seemed close, to raise money for weapons and to persuade local Christians not to cooperate with the Germans. About ten members served in the Jewish Police. On 20 April 1942 the organisation became known to the Germans, and Dvoretzky and six others fled to the forest. He was killed soon afterwards. The museum describes an ambush by non-Jewish partisans. The Jewish Virtual Library's chronology says he was shot by Soviet partisans after refusing to hand over his pistol.

On 29 April the Germans arrested the Judenrat. At dawn the next day the ghetto woke to shooting. The Germans announced through the council that all Jews must report to the old cemetery, which lay inside the ghetto, and their collaborators began driving people from their houses, beating, kicking and shooting those who resisted. A selection followed. According to the museum, the district commissar chose more than 1,000 people, mostly women, children and the elderly, and had them escorted to the Kurpyash Forest south of town, where pits were ready. They were shot in groups of 20. The museum says German and local Polish police forces carried it out. Survivors' accounts in the memorial book spell the forest "Kurfish" and name the district commissar as Taub or Traube. Those accounts also speak of White Russian policemen.

The survivors' accounts give the day a human scale that the summaries cannot. The Germans split the crowd left and right. Lize Kaplinsky wrote that she stood in the left-hand row, which meant death, until she showed a hospital pass to an executioner she called Hick, who sent her "to Novolunie, to peel potatoes". Another account says that at the pits a woman hugged her ten-year-old son and told him not to be afraid because it did not hurt. Another writer says that after about ten hours of gunfire the town went quiet. The Jewish Virtual Library's chronology says twelve hundred Jews were killed in the town that spring.
After the shooting the ghetto was made smaller, and the remaining Jews were squeezed into its oldest and narrowest houses, one account says.

The second operation began on 6 August and lasted three days, the museum says, because many Jews had hidden in prepared bunkers. The museum says the victims were shot into three mass graves in the Jewish cemetery, with roughly 1,000 in each. The Jewish Virtual Library's chronology says 3,000 were murdered and that 600 escaped, more than 100 of whom formed a partisan unit.

The memorial book describes the morning. A boy of twelve, Kalmen Mnuskin, wrote that he woke to the noise of a truck and then a single shot, and heard shouted orders for the Jews to come out. His family split up to hide. He spent days in a cellar that was really a covered toilet pit, built for three or four people, with eleven crammed inside. On the third night he and the others crawled out and tried to reach the old cemetery. His parents and three younger brothers, he learned, were no longer in their cellar.

Another survivor described being put on a truck that stood facing the cemetery, then driven back to the marketplace. There, the writer says, people were laid out in rows on their knees, faces to the pavement, and Germans walked the rows taking boots, watches and rings. The district commissar stood nearby with machine guns and a camera, according to this account. The count at the end was 213, which the writer set against 4,000 Jews in Zhetl. They were shut in the cinema, then moved to Nowogródek.

The museum says slightly more than 200 craftsmen were transferred to the ghetto at Nowogródek, and that a few hundred who had been in hiding got away once the shooting stopped. Some formed a family camp in the Nakryshki Forest and lived there until liberation. The museum describes this as the end of the Jewish community of Zdziecioł.

The totals differ by source, and the museum itself gives a range for August. For the first action, the museum says more than 1,000, and the chronology says twelve hundred. A survivor who wrote about a man who escaped from the graves put the number murdered in one set of graves at 500, which cannot easily be tied to either action. For August, the museum says 2,000 to 3,000 and the chronology says 3,000.

The Soviet Extraordinary State Commission took a different line. According to a footnote in the museum's entry, its report dated the second massacre to July 1942 and put the total of Jewish victims at 3,500. The commission also dated the ghetto's creation to 1941, with up to 4,500 inmates, whereas an oral-history interviewee quoted by the museum placed its creation in February 1942. The same archive file, the museum says, establishes the names of 1,601 victims. The museum also points to a list of the Jews murdered in 1942 in a regional volume published in Minsk in 1997.

After Dvoretzky's flight, a partisan detachment of more than 100 Jews formed near the town, called the Zheteler detachment. Anyone wishing to join first had to obtain a gun. It had three platoons, led by Hershl Kaplinski, Jonah Midvetsky and Shalom Ogulnik, and women served as nurses, cooks and clerks, with a few taking part in fighting. The base was about 20 kilometres from the town, in the Lipichanski Forest, and the unit worked with Soviet partisan groups, among them the Orlanski detachment commanded by Nikolai Vakhonin. The museum says the partisans attacked railway lines, and that a mine invented by Yisrael Bousel was used to derail trains. Bousel was posthumously named a Hero of the Soviet Union.

The Zheteler unit also took revenge on local collaborators. On 10 September 1942, in the village of Molery, it killed two collaborators and then told the village elder why. Many Jews who tried to reach the forest from the labour camps were caught on the way, the museum says. In December 1942 German units surrounded the Lipichanski Forest in a prolonged operation, according to a memoir of the partisan hospital by Sholem Gerling, which described bitter fighting, many wounded and typhus among the fighters. The chronology records that Hirsch Kaplinski, who had survived the August massacre, was killed in combat during a German attack on the forest.

The Jews of Zhetl who had been sent to Nowogródek were not safe there either. One account in the memorial book says that after "the slaughter of May 1943", in which many Zhetl Jews were killed, the idea of a collective escape took hold. Its organisers, according to the writer, were Dr. Kagan from Baranovitch and a Zhetl carpenter, Itchke Dvoretzky. A tunnel was dug from a building the Zhetl Jews called the "Zhetl Closet". The writer gives its dimensions as 187 metres long, 2.5 metres deep, 90 centimetres wide and 70 centimetres high, and says the diggers worked on their knees. The soil was hidden in attics and between double walls, and wood for the supports was stolen from the carpentry shop.

The same account says 235 people escaped, the last Jews of Zhetl together with the last Jews from the Nowogródek ghetto. They went through one at a time, from a prepared list, and the first and last were young men with weapons. The writer says a few Jews stayed behind, too frightened to enter, and were killed. It says the fate of those who got out varied. Most made for Zhetl, and almost all of them were caught and shot, some by Germans and some by partisans. Only a small number reached the Lipitchaner forest, the writer says. A second survivor, Moishe Mendl Leyzerovitch, estimated the tunnel at 200 metres, said the work took ten weeks, and said that only a few dozen of those who left it survived. He was in the forest near Stolptz until the Soviets liberated the area in July 1944. Where the two accounts differ on length and time, both are the memories of people who were there.

The museum lists where records on the town's Jews are held: German federal archive files, the national archive file of Belarus that holds the Soviet commission's report, an oral history in its own collection and a file in Israel. For the wider story of the town it points to the 1957 memorial book, Pinkes Zshetl, edited by Baruch Kaplinski, and a later Israeli volume marking sixty years since the community's destruction in 1942. The translated testimonies on JewishGen come from that memorial literature. The museum entry names some of the first victims, among them Etl Ovsievitz and her daughter Dina, killed at Nowojelnia in July 1941, and Libe Gercowski; the translated testimonies record the fathers, mothers and children whose last words survivors set down in print.
